chapter.name: EIGRP
chapter.description: EIGRP fundamentals, DUAL, neighbor formation, metrics, and verification

questions.question: What kind of routing protocol is EIGRP and what does DUAL stand for?
questions.answer: EIGRP is Cisco's proprietary enhanced distance-vector protocol (hybrid of distance-vector and link-state traits) that uses DUAL — Diffusing Update Algorithm — for loop-free, fast convergence by pre-computing alternate paths.
questions.explanation: DUAL lets EIGRP converge quickly: as long as a feasible successor exists, failures are handled locally with no recalculation. Metric components are bandwidth and delay by default.
acceptableAnswers: cisco proprietary enhanced distance vector using dual diffusing update algorithm
hybrid protocol, dual = diffusing update algorithm

questions.question: What is the administrative distance of internal EIGRP routes and of re-distributed (external) EIGRP routes?
choices: Internal 90, external 170
Internal 110, external 170
Internal 90, external 120
Internal 5, external 170
questions.answer: Internal 90, external 170
questions.explanation: Internal EIGRP routes (AD 90) beat OSPF (110) and RIP (120); external EIGRP routes drop to 170. The different ADs also support EIGRP summarization with 'administrative distance' control.

questions.question: EIGRP is limited to Cisco equipment because it is a proprietary protocol — other vendors can never interoperate with it.
questions.answer: false
questions.explanation: Cisco published EIGRP as an informational RFC (7868) so other vendors can implement it, but in practice interoperability outside Cisco ecosystems is rare.

questions.question: What multicast address does EIGRP use for its hello packets and what protocol type does it use?
questions.answer: 224.0.0.10 with IP protocol number 88 (IPPROTO_EIGRP). Reliable transports (updates/queries/replies) on point-to-point links also use unicast to the neighbor's IP.
questions.explanation: Hellos are unreliable multicasts every 5 s (hello hold time 15 s); on NBMA, neighbors can be manually defined for unicast hellos. RTP (Reliable Transport Protocol) handles the five packet types: hello, update, query, reply, ACK.

questions.question: Which two factors are used in the default EIGRP metric calculation?
choices: Bandwidth and delay
Bandwidth and hop count
Delay and load
Load and reliability
questions.answer: Bandwidth and delay
questions.explanation: The full formula uses bandwidth (lowest along path), delay (cumulative), plus load and reliability — but by default only bandwidth and delay are used (K1=1, K3=1, others 0).

questions.question: Write the default EIGRP metric formula.
questions.answer: Metric = [10^7 / (lowest bandwidth in kbps) + (sum of delays in tens of microseconds)] x 256, i.e. metric = [(10,000,000 / BW) + delay] * 256 with loading (K2), reliability (K4) factors included only if their K-values are non-zero.
questions.explanation: Example: a 10 Mb path with 20,000 usec delay = [(10^7/10000) + 2000] x 256 = 3000 x 256 = 768,000. Lower metric is preferred.
acceptableAnswers: 10 million divided by slowest bandwidth plus cumulative delay times 256
k1 bandwidth plus k3 delay multiplied by 256
hints: What value multiplies the final sum?
Which link's bandwidth — fastest or slowest — enters the formula?

questions.question: When EIGRP path selection is deciding between routes to the same destination, it prefers the path with the lowest composite metric, regardless of hop count.
questions.answer: true
questions.explanation: Hop count is not part of the default metric; EIGRP uses bandwidth/delay (and optionally load/reliability). A 50-hop gigabit path can beat a 2-hop T1 path.

questions.question: State the EIGRP Feasibility Condition.
questions.answer: A route can become a feasible successor only if its reported distance (RD — the neighbor's advertised distance to the destination) is lower than the current feasible distance (FD — the best metric to the destination). If RD >= FD, no feasible successor exists and DUAL must run a diffusing computation.
questions.explanation: This guarantees loop-free alternatives: the alternate path's cost must be strictly lower than the best path's cost from the perspective of the downstream neighbor.
acceptableAnswers: reported distance must be less than feasible distance
the neighbor's advertised distance must be lower than the best metric
hints: Symbols: what is RD and what is FD?

questions.question: Router A's FD to 10.0.0.0/24 is 300. Neighbors advertise: B=280, C=300, D=350. Which neighbors are feasible successors?
choices: Only B (RD 280 < 300)
B and D (RD below and equal to FD)
B, C and D since all have routes
None — only the successor is a feasible successor
questions.answer: Only B (RD 280 < 300)
questions.explanation: Feasibility Condition: RD must be strictly LESS than FD. C's RD equals FD and D's RD is greater, so they can only be used after a diffusing computation (active state).

questions.question: What is the difference between a successor and a feasible successor in EIGRP?
questions.answer: A successor is the neighbor on the best (lowest-metric) path to a destination and is used for forwarding traffic and entered in the routing table. A feasible successor is a backup neighbor whose reported distance meets the feasibility condition — it is kept in the topology table for instant local failover with no diffusing computation.
questions.explanation: show ip eigrp topology shows both: successors are the 'via' entries with P (passive) at the top; the topology table stores every DUAL state, both passive (P) and active (A).
acceptableAnswers: successor is the best path neighbor, feasible successor is a loop free backup neighbor
successor for forwarding, feasible successor for instant backup
hints: Which one enables instant failover without querying?

questions.question: What do the states 'Passive' and 'Active' mean in the EIGRP topology table?
choices: Passive = route stable and in use; Active = DUAL actively searching (querying) for a new path because no feasible successor existed
Passive = route installed in the forwarding table; Active = route from a passive interface
Passive = valid backup; Active = candidate successor
Passive = link up; Active = the route is being redistributed
questions.answer: Passive = route stable and in use; Active = DUAL actively searching (querying) for a new path because no feasible successor existed
questions.explanation: A route that must go Active triggers queries to neighbors; if DUAL finds no feasible successor the route becomes Active until replies arrive — a stuck-in-active (SIA) situation arises if neighbors fail to reply.

questions.question: What does 'Stuck in Active' (SIA) mean and what usually causes it?
questions.answer: SIA means a neighbor failed to answer EIGRP queries within the active-time limit (default 3 minutes) while DUAL was searching for a new path. Common causes: CPU saturation, congested/unreliable links dropping reliable-transport packets, or asymmetric MTU issues.
questions.explanation: SIA events can cascade: a neighbor that is stuck stays in the topology table and the local router keeps waiting, sometimes causing flapping and route loss. Troubleshooting focuses on the physical/logical link quality.
acceptableAnswers: neighbor failed to answer queries within active time
stuck in active means query replies never came
hints: Which DUAL state does the route enter?
Which packet type carries the search?

questions.question: How do EIGRP neighbors form?
questions.answer: Routers exchange hellos on the interface (every 5 s, multicast 224.0.0.10). Once they see a matching AS number and K-values, they exchange full routing information via reliable updates; each update is acknowledged. After the initial exchange, only changes trigger updates (event-driven).
questions.explanation: Unlike OSPF there are no adjacency state machines to speak of — show ip eigrp neighbors lists them; a neighbor is formed approximately when hellos are exchanged successfully.
acceptableAnswers: hellos on the same as with matching k values, then full updates with acks

questions.question: Which of these does NOT prevent EIGRP neighbor formation on a directly connected link?
choices: A different router ID on each side
Different EIGRP AS numbers
Mismatched K-values
Passive interface on one side
questions.answer: A different router ID on each side
questions.explanation: Router IDs merely need to be unique per instance — mismatched AS or K-values, or a passive interface (no hellos sent), break adjacency. Timers do NOT need to match in EIGRP (asymmetric failure still works).

questions.question: EIGRP hello and hold timers do not need to match between neighbors for an adjacency to form.
questions.answer: true
questions.explanation: Unlike OSPF, EIGRP allows mismatched timers: each side uses its own hold time to time out the peer. AS number, K-values, and availability of hellos are what matter.

questions.question: Write the commands to enable EIGRP AS 100 on a router, advertise only 10.1.1.0/24, and disable auto-summarization.
questions.answer:
R1(config)# router eigrp 100
R1(config-router)# no auto-summary
R1(config-router)# network 10.1.1.0
questions.explanation: With the classic configuration, 'network' matches the classful boundary unless auto-summary is disabled; 10.1.1.0 matches interface 10.1.1.x. Enable EIGRP per-interface with 'ip eigrp 100' only, or covered by a network statement.

questions.question: What is the effect of the 'passive-interface' command under EIGRP?
choices: The interface stops sending and receiving EIGRP hello packets, so no neighbors form on it, but any already-learned routes stay in the table
The interface stops routing all traffic
It shrinks the hello timer to 1 second
It only suppresses multicast but keeps unicast neighbors
questions.answer: The interface stops sending and receiving EIGRP hello packets, so no neighbors form on it, but any already-learned routes stay in the table
questions.explanation: 'passive-interface default' makes all interfaces passive; individual 'no passive-interface' re-enables specific ones. Very common to stop routes leaking toward LAN segments.

questions.question: Which command shows the EIGRP neighbor table — including the current timers toward each neighbor?
questions.answer: show ip eigrp neighbors
questions.explanation: Columns: Hold (time remaining), Uptime, SRTT and RTO (reliability timers), Q Cnt, Seq Num. Use 'show ip eigrp neighbors detail' for more, like passive-interface status.

questions.question: Which command shows the EIGRP topology table with successors, feasible successors, and DUAL states (P/A)?
questions.answer: show ip eigrp topology
questions.explanation: First line per route shows FD and route state Passive/Active; 'via' lines name the neighbor, its RD and, if it is a feasible successor, '(FD is ...)' markers. Add '/all-links' to see every path including those violating the feasibility condition.

questions.question: Which command shows EIGRP route entries in the routing table along with their source and whether the path is internal or external?
questions.answer: show ip route eigrp
questions.explanation: Displays lines prefixed with 'D' (internal) or 'D EX' (external), together with '[90/4373760]' style AD/metric values.

questions.question: Which command shows EIGRP traffic statistics and the number of packets sent/received of each type?
questions.answer: show ip eigrp traffic
questions.explanation: Breaks down hellos, updates, queries, replies, acks, and SIA queries sent and received, plus queued counts.

questions.question: After adding a router, the neighbor table shows the neighbor but no routes are exchanged. What is the most likely cause?
questions.answer: Auto-summary (default on older IOS) collapsed the networks to classful boundaries on one or both sides, so the routes were summarized to a different classful network (e.g. 10.0.0.0) and dropped by the remote side.
questions.explanation: Classic EIGRP defaults to auto-summary; 'no auto-summary' under router eigrp fixes this.
symptoms: No EIGRP routes appear in show ip route
show ip eigrp topology has entries summarized at classful boundaries
questions.topology: Two routers connected via GigabitEthernet0/0 on 10.1.1.0/30 with subnet 10.1.2.0/24 behind R1
questions.showOutput:
R1# show ip eigrp topology
P 10.0.0.0/8, 1 successors, FD is 28160 via R2
hints: Which EIGRP default creates classful advertisements?
Where are the routes listed — does the destination match the actual subnet?

questions.question: A remote site's link is flapping: the neighbor table is empty every few minutes, then repopulates. What could cause intermittent EIGRP neighbors, and what do you check first?
questions.answer: Check physical/logical link quality (errors, drops, MTU), hello/hold reachability, and any ACL or firewall dropping protocol 88; common cause is packet loss exceeding the 15s hold time on a congested link — verify with show ip eigrp neighbors (watch uptime) and interface error counters/underruns.
questions.explanation: If reliable packets are lost, EIGRP marks routes active and re-queries; flapping neighbor tables usually mean hellos being dropped intermittently — CPU, link errors, or L3 filtering (ACL/permit protocol 88).
symptoms: show ip eigrp topology shows routes occasionally going Active (A)
questions.topology: WAN router pair separated by a provider link with visible interface error counters
questions.showOutput:
R1# show ip eigrp neighbors
H Address    Interface   Hold Uptime  SRTT RTO Q Seq
1 10.0.0.2   Gi0/1       2    01:12:34 12  120  0  44
R1# show interface Gi0/1 | include error|CRC
  input errors: 1482, CRC: 1482
acceptableAnswers: packet loss on the wan link
hints: What packet type keeps the neighbor table alive?
What does the CRC counter tell you?
